name: Physicalism
statement: Everything that exists is physical, including the mind, which is grounded wholly in the brain.
statementAccent: including the mind, which is grounded wholly in the brain
meaning: Physicalism is the metaphysical thesis that everything that exists is physical, or is entirely dependent on, determined by, or supervenient on the physical. In the philosophy of mind, it is the view that the mind is physical, so that mental states are, or are wholly grounded in, physical states such as states of the brain. Physicalism is roughly synonymous with materialism and is the modern successor to it; the term was introduced by members of the Vienna Circle to tie the view to physics rather than to an older notion of matter, so that it encompasses not only matter but everything physics posits, including energy, fields, and forces. Physicalism comes in several varieties within the philosophy of mind. Reductive physicalism, or the type-identity theory, holds that mental state-types just are brain state-types, as in the claim that pain is the firing of C-fibers. Functionalism defines mental states by their causal roles and allows them to be realized in different physical systems, a way of being physicalist without strict identity. Non-reductive physicalism holds that mental properties supervene on but are not reducible to physical properties. Eliminative materialism holds that the mental states of common-sense psychology do not really exist. Physicalism is the dominant, mainstream position in contemporary analytic philosophy of mind and the metaphysics of science.
mechanism: Physicalism holds that the physical facts fix all the facts, so that once the physical nature of the world is settled, everything else, including the mental, is thereby settled. A central way of making this precise is supervenience: the mental supervenes on the physical if there can be no mental difference without a physical difference, so any world that is a physical duplicate of ours is a duplicate in every respect, including the mental. Within this framework, physicalists differ over how the mental relates to the physical. The reductive physicalist, or type-identity theorist, holds that each type of mental state is identical to some type of physical state, so pain, for example, just is a particular kind of neural activity. The functionalist defines mental states by their causal role, their relations to inputs, outputs, and other states, which allows the same mental state to be realized in different physical substrates, a way of remaining physicalist while denying strict type-identity. The non-reductive physicalist accepts that mental properties supervene on the physical without being reducible to it, so the mental is physically grounded but not simply identical to any physical type. The eliminative materialist takes the most radical line, holding that the categories of common-sense psychology are a mistaken theory and that the states they posit do not exist. Physicalists support the thesis by appeal to the causal closure of the physical, the correlation of mind and brain, and the success and parsimony of physical science.

examples.text: Physicalism holds that mental states are or are wholly grounded in physical states, such as states of the brain.
The mental supervenes on the physical: there can be no mental difference without a physical difference.
Physicalists argue that every physical effect has a sufficient physical cause, leaving no causal work for a non-physical mind.

whyItMatters: Physicalism is the dominant position in contemporary philosophy of mind and a foundational commitment of the modern scientific worldview, holding that everything, including the mind, is ultimately physical. Its importance lies in unifying our understanding of the world under the ontology of physics, so that the mind, like everything else, is seen as part of the natural, physical order and in principle amenable to scientific explanation, rather than as a separate immaterial realm. Physicalism frames the central debate of philosophy of mind against dualism, and its various forms, type-identity theory, functionalism, non-reductive physicalism, and eliminative materialism, map the main ways of understanding how the mental relates to the physical. It is closely tied to neuroscience and cognitive science, which seek to explain mental phenomena in terms of the brain, and to arguments from the causal closure of the physical and the parsimony of physical explanation. At the same time, physicalism must confront the deepest challenges of consciousness, the knowledge argument, the hard problem, qualia, and philosophical zombies, which question whether it can account for subjective experience.

limits: Physicalism is the mainstream view but faces serious and unresolved challenges, principally from consciousness. The knowledge argument holds that someone who knew every physical fact about color could still learn something new on first seeing red, suggesting there are non-physical facts about experience; the hard problem of consciousness asks why physical processes are accompanied by subjective experience at all; philosophical zombies, physical duplicates of us lacking consciousness, are invoked to suggest experience is over and above the physical; and the explanatory gap marks the difficulty of explaining qualia in physical terms. Physicalists have replies, such as the ability hypothesis and the phenomenal concepts strategy, and notably Frank Jackson, who devised the knowledge argument, later became a physicalist, but the challenges remain live. Physicalism is also a family of positions, from type-identity to eliminativism, that disagree among themselves.
misreadings: Physicalism is not the same as old-fashioned materialism about matter; it ties the view to all of physics, including energy and fields, and is the broader modern successor term. It is not a single theory but a family, including type-identity, functionalism, non-reductive physicalism, and eliminativism, which disagree among themselves. And its dominance does not mean it has explained consciousness, since the knowledge argument, the hard problem, and qualia remain live challenges, so treating physicalism as mere matter-materialism, as one uniform view, or as having solved consciousness, misreads the dominant but contested framework of philosophy of mind.
origin: The metaphysical thesis that everything is physical, the modern successor to materialism named by the Vienna Circle; in philosophy of mind, the dominant view that the mind is grounded wholly in the physical.
